title: Trump Signs Greenland Security Deal as Golden Dome and Two New US Bases Move Into Arctic
subhead: The US, Denmark and Greenland signed a deal Tuesday ending a months-long standoff, codifying a larger US military footprint on the island — including a 'Golden Dome' missile shield and two new bases — while handing Arctic security oversight to NATO.

sections.heading: Greenland Deal Signed: Golden Dome and Two US Bases
sections.body:
President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed a security agreement on Tuesday at the UN General Assembly in New York, resolving the standoff that erupted after Trump repeatedly threatened to acquire the semi-autonomous Danish territory. The deal codifies a larger US military presence on Greenland while stopping short of annexation, per SCMP and Reuters.

The released text says the US can establish a 'Golden Dome' defense system in Greenland as a shield against ballistic missile threats — the Arctic island lies on the shortest route from Europe to North America and hosts the northernmost US military base. Trump said the US will build two major military bases in Greenland under the deal. Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen told broadcaster TV2 that responsibility for Arctic security would now, to a large extent, fall to NATO rather than being solely Danish or American; a NATO spokesperson welcomed the agreement as strengthening 'security, stability and cooperation' in the region, Defense News and Reuters report.
sections.whyItMatters: It converts eight months of coercive diplomacy and NATO-infighting over Greenland's future into a signed framework that expands US missile-defense and basing reach to the top of the globe while keeping Danish sovereignty intact — and hands the alliance a formal, if vaguely defined, role in the Arctic.

sections.heading: AUKUS Pillar 2: US Mk 48 Torpedo Launched From Royal Navy UUV
sections.body:
The Royal Navy successfully launched a US Navy Mk 48 Heavyweight Torpedo from the British Excalibur uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) on Sept. 13 at the British Underwater Test & Evaluation Centre in Scotland, Defense News reports. The trial validates a major achievement under AUKUS Pillar 2, the US-UK-Australia pact enabling interoperable UUV payload systems.

The test 'validated the mechanical, electrical, and software integration of a U.S. kinetic payload onto an allied autonomous vessel, proving that allied forces can rapidly achieve weapon interchangeability,' the Navy said. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle called it 'a historic first for allied undersea warfare.' The Excalibur, the Royal Navy's first uncrewed submarine unveiled in May 2025, has no torpedo tubes but a large central payload bay; the roughly 40-foot UUV carried the 19-foot Mk 48 in a hull-mounted cradle. The Mk 48 MOD 7 results from a Joint Development Program with the Royal Australian Navy, per Navy Lookout and Defense News.
sections.whyItMatters: It is the first concrete demonstration that an allied uncrewed submarine can deliver a US heavyweight torpedo — a proof of concept for weapon interchangeability across three navies' unmanned fleets, and a marker for how AUKUS Pillar 2 wants to scale undersea combat power without new crewed hulls.

sections.heading: CENTCOM as a Battle Lab for Unmanned Systems
sections.body:
US forces are now operating unmanned systems 'on, above, and below the sea' in the Middle East, a US official told Military Times, as the region has become a proving ground for robot warfare. Three Corsair unmanned surface vessels (USVs) struck the Bandar Abbas naval base in Iran in July — the first time American forces have employed sea drones in combat, CENTCOM confirmed, Defense News reports.

The same systems have proven dual-use: after a US Army helicopter went down near the Strait of Hormuz in June, an unmanned Navy vessel from Task Force 59 helped recover two service members. The Navy stood up Task Force 59 in 2021 to accelerate unmanned and AI integration, later adding Task Group 59.1 for operational deployment, and its February 2026 Fighting Instructions assign specific roles to unmanned platforms. CNA's Joshua Tallis said real-world use gives the Navy an 'unrivaled opportunity' to refine how it commands and sustains robotic systems.
sections.whyItMatters: A year of war has compressed what was a laboratory exercise into combat operations — with USVs delivering strikes on Iranian infrastructure and unmanned craft performing search-and-rescue — validating CENTCOM as both the test range and the operational test of unmanned warfare at scale.

sections.heading: US Destroyer Fleet Stretched as Middle East Demands Mount
sections.body:
As of Sept. 14, 15 US guided-missile destroyers were concentrated in the Middle East — two in the Red Sea and 13 in the Arabian Sea — as US forces conduct operations against Iran, per CENTCOM and the US Naval Institute fleet tracker, Defense News reports. The Arleigh Burke-class USS Stout departed Norfolk Monday to begin deployment after months of training.

The tempo is familiar: the USS Carney logged 235 days deployed in 2023-24 and 51 engagements against Houthi-launched weapons — a pace former CNO Adm. Lisa Franchetti compared to direct fleet-vs-fleet action in World War II. The renewed demand collides with a maintenance backlog: a December 2025 CBO analysis found Arleigh Burke overhauls begun between 2011-2024 ran 26% longer than scheduled on average, and DDG-51s are projected to spend more than nine years — about 27% of planned service life — in maintenance, Defense News and CBO report.
sections.whyItMatters: The DDG force is being asked to sustain near-continuous Middle East presence while the CBO documents that the industrial and maintenance base can't keep the class on schedule — a classic fleet-readiness squeeze that will shape procurement and shipyard investment decisions.

sections.heading: Pentagon's Weapons Speed-Up Effort Stays Opaque
sections.body:
Twenty-six days after Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg's Aug. 26 deadline for defense firms to propose faster weapons production, the Pentagon has not disclosed how many companies responded or what timelines they offered, Defense News/Military Times report. The Aug. 5 memo identified 16 critical programs slated for accelerated production, with responses meant to inform the fiscal 2028 budget request.

The pressure stems from the Iran war's toll on stockpiles: a CSIS analysis found Patriot interceptor inventories fell from about 2,330 pre-war to between 759 and 827 by late July, and THAAD stocks from 452 to between 234 and 278 — with production timelines of roughly 42 months for PAC-3 MSE and 53 months for THAAD interceptors. Lockheed Martin and General Dynamics declined to detail their submissions to the Pentagon, though Lockheed separately announced its first PAC-3 MSE housing components from GM Defense arrived 22 days after the firms signed a production contract.
sections.whyItMatters: The Pentagon is asking industry to surge production of air-defense and precision munitions after a war exposed depleted interceptor stocks, but the results of that surge request remain classified — leaving Congress and the market to guess whether the defense-industrial base can actually deliver the timelines Washington now needs.

sections.heading: China Upgrades Djibouti Base With SIGINT Gear
sections.body:
China has upgraded its military base in Djibouti with communications equipment a US think tank says is 'likely enhancing' the PLA's ability to collect signals intelligence (SIGINT), potentially giving it visibility into foreign military operations in Djibouti and the wider Middle East, SCMP reports. Commercial imagery reveals two new communication sites built near foreign militaries' bases in East Africa.

The facility, opened in 2017 as a naval support hub, has become a center for Chinese operations in the Gulf of Aden and Red Sea. The upgrade could matter more given US Air Force budget documents describe nearby Chabelley Airfield as the only location in East Africa from which armed ISR assets are authorized to operate. In August, Japan began flying P-1 maritime patrol aircraft from its own Djibouti facility for counter-piracy and Middle East intelligence-gathering.
sections.whyItMatters: As the US-Iran conflict draws foreign militaries to the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, a modest-looking upgrade at China's East African base signals Beijing's intent to extend electronic surveillance over the same waters Western navies are operating in — a quiet build-out of the region's signals battlefield.

sections.heading: NATO Eastern Flank: Germany Airlifts Eurofighters, Latvia Buys Czech Howitzers
sections.body:
Germany will send four Eurofighter Typhoons and several dozen personnel to Latvia's Lielvarde air base for a week spanning late September and early October to secure airspace during Latvia's Oct. 3 parliamentary election, Defense News reports — an unusual short, election-focused mission under NATO's enhanced Air Policing rather than the routine four-month rotations, prompted by repeated drone incursions from Russia and Belarus. Italian NATO jets in Lithuania shot down a suspected Russian-made drone this week, the first drone downed in Lithuanian airspace.

Separately, Latvia's government approved buying Czech Morana 155 mm self-propelled howitzers from Excalibur Army (Czechoslovak Group), reversing a June 2025 letter of intent with Sweden's BAE Systems Bofors for Archer systems. Riga cited better cost, delivery terms and local industry involvement. Latvia's 2026 defense budget is a record 4.91% of GDP (€2.16 billion), funding indirect-fire support as a key capability project, per Defense News.
sections.whyItMatters: Two Baltic moves show how the eastern flank is hardening in practice — NATO air policing adapting to a drone-threatened election, and a small ally walking away from a major Western program for a cheaper Czech alternative that brings industrial offsets — evidence of the flexibility European procurement now has under elevated defense budgets.

bottomLine: Tuesday's signing of the Greenland security deal was the day's defining event: it converts the US-Denmark-Greenland confrontation over the Arctic into a signed framework that plants Golden Dome ballistic-missile defense and two new US bases on the island while formally handing Arctic security oversight to NATO. Beneath that, the defense-industrial and force-readiness story continued along familiar but accelerating lines — AUKUS demonstrated the first US heavyweight torpedo launch from a British uncrewed submarine, CENTCOM kept showing unmanned systems moving from experiments to combat operations, US destroyers strain against a documented maintenance backlog, and the Pentagon's classified push for faster weapons production collides with CSIS numbers showing depleted interceptor stocks. Beijing's quiet SIGINT upgrade at Djibouti adds a non-Western dimension to an increasingly contested Red Sea signals environment.
sources: Defense News, Reuters, SCMP, Military Times, Navy Lookout, CSIS, CBO, US Naval Institute, CENTCOM
